readerTitle: Three numbers on the table: pricing a new candle
caseNote: 가상 사례 (생활용품 회사 안의 신규 캔들 브랜드 팀, 기프트숍 체인 바이어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 원가는 바닥, 경쟁 제품은 기준점, 고객 가치는 천장. 가격은 하나의 공식이 아니라 세 숫자가 각자 맡은 역할을 함께 보고 정한다.
misconception: 원가에 정해진 마진을 붙이면 '공정하고 안전한' 가격이 나온다.

sources.text: 가격 전략의 표준 개념 (원가 기반, 경쟁 기반, 가치 기반 가격)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산: 소매가 $24 → 도매가 $12(소매점이 판매가의 절반을 가져간다는 가정) − 제조원가 $6 = 브랜드 몫 $6. 소매가 $32 → 도매가 $16 − $6 = $10. 10 ÷ 6 ≈ 1.67배.
'소매점이 도매가의 약 두 배로 판다'는 가정은 여러 소매 업종의 흔한 관행으로만 설명했고, 특정 비율을 업계 통계로 제시하지 않았습니다. 카드에도 'in this example'로 적었습니다.
5번 카드의 선물 고객 테스트 결과는 가상 사례입니다. 실제 연구나 통계로 읽히지 않도록 구체적 비율을 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Three numbers on the table: pricing a new candle
body: A home-goods company gives a small team one job: launch a candle brand and sell it through gift-shop chains.
Three numbers land on the table. Each candle costs **$6** to make. Similar candles on the shelf sell for $18 to $40. And finance has already filled in a price: $24.

image.label: Three sticky notes beside a candle: $6, $18–$40, $24
image.brief: 회의 테이블 위에 유리병 캔들 하나. 옆에 포스트잇 세 장: "Cost $6", "Shelf $18–$40", "Finance $24". 따뜻한 조명, 3D 클레이 스타일. 실제 브랜드 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: How do you set the shelf price?
body: You lead the launch team. The candle has a hand-poured look and comes in a gift box. Most early buyers say they would give it as a present.
Finance wants a decision this week.

options.text: Use finance's $24: double the cost to sell to stores, and stores double it again
options.feedback: That's **cost-plus pricing**. It guarantees you never sell below cost, but it ignores what gift buyers would pay, so it can leave money on the table.

options.text: Price at $28, the middle of the shelf
options.feedback: That's **competitor-based pricing**. It keeps you from looking strange, but the middle of the shelf is an average, not your customer.

options.text: Start with what gift buyers would pay, then check it against cost and the shelf
options.feedback: That's **value-based pricing**, with cost as the floor and competitors as a reality check. It takes more work, but each number does its own job.

cards.title: Where a $24 candle's money goes.
body: In this example, the store keeps half of what the shopper pays. So the team's share is small: **$6** per candle to pay for marketing, salaries and profit.

cards.title: Three numbers, three different jobs.
body: **Cost** is the floor. Below $6 to make, plus the store's share, every sale loses money. It tells you where not to go, not where to stop.
**The shelf** is the reference. Shoppers compare you with the candles beside you.
**Value to the buyer** is the ceiling. A gift has to look generous, so gift buyers often care less about a few dollars.

image.label: A price range: floor, reference band, ceiling
image.brief: 세로 눈금자 인포그래픽. 아래쪽 "Floor: cost", 가운데 띠 "Reference: the shelf", 위쪽 "Ceiling: value to the buyer". 가격이 이 범위 안 어디에 놓일지 화살표로 표시.

cards.softwareNote: A new app works the same way. Server costs set a low floor, rival apps set the reference, and the time or money it saves a customer sets the ceiling. Because the floor is so low, cost-plus thinking often underprices software badly.

cards.title: Gift buyers didn't flinch at $32.
body: The team put the boxed candle on a test shelf with gift candles at $30 to $40. At $32, shoppers picked it about as often as at $24.
At $32, the store buys at $16. The brand keeps **$10** per candle instead of $6, about two-thirds more, from the same wax and the same jar.
Cost-plus would never have found that $4. It only looks down at the floor.

cards.title: The ceiling only holds if everything says "gift."
body: Value isn't fixed. It depends on the box, the scent, the label and where the candle sits. Put a $32 candle in a plain wrapper and shoppers see a pricey everyday candle.
The store also matters. Its staff and shelf choices shape what your candle is compared with.
And launch prices stick. Starting high is easier than raising prices later, but only if the product earns it.

cards.title: The buyer offers two shelves.
body: A gift-shop chain's buyer likes the candle. She offers a spot in the everyday home aisle, next to $18 candles, or a smaller spot in the gift section, next to $35 boxed sets.

options.text: Everyday aisle, priced at $24 to move more units
options.feedback: You'd sell more, but you'd keep $6 a candle instead of $10 and train shoppers to see it as an everyday item.
The neighbors make $32 look fair, which is **competitor-based pricing** working for you, and gift buyers are the ones who value it most.
Next to $18 candles, $32 looks overpriced. The shelf reference works against the value you built.

cards.title: Let each number do its own job.
body: This lesson used three pricing ideas together: **cost-plus** set the floor, **competitor-based** pricing set the reference, and **value-based** pricing found the ceiling.
**Try it today:** pick one product. Write its floor, its closest shelf neighbors, and what its best customer would pay. Where does your current price sit?
